must_remember: Random thermal velocities of free electrons in a conductor are of the order of $10^5\text{ m/s}$, whereas their drift velocity is extremely small, typically of the order of $10^{-4}\text{ m/s}$.
The microscopic form of Ohm's law relates current density $J$ and electric field $E$ as $J = \sigma E$, where $\sigma$ is electrical conductivity.
Mobility $\mu$ is defined as the magnitude of drift velocity per unit electric field, given by $\mu = \frac{v_d}{E} = \frac{e \tau}{m}$.
Electrical resistivity is inversely proportional to relaxation time and free electron density: $\rho = \frac{m}{n e^2 \tau}$.
Electric signals propagate through a conductor at a speed close to the speed of light, while the actual drift speed of electrons is very slow.

glossary.meaning: The average uniform speed with which free electrons get drifted towards the positive terminal under the influence of an applied electric field.
The average time interval between two successive collisions of free electrons with the positive ion cores in a metal lattice.
The magnitude of drift velocity acquired per unit electric field, serving as a measure of how quickly a charge carrier moves.
The electric current flowing per unit cross-sectional area normal to the current, expressed as $J = n e v_d$.
The average distance traveled by a free electron between two successive collisions.
